header.intro: Each project below is presented in three layers — a non-technical TL;DR for stakeholders, a visual workflow showing how the system thinks, and a deep technical breakdown for engineers. 18 projects spanning NLP pipelines at a global bank, knowledge-graph RAG for legal AI, real estate analytics, career AI platforms, fraud detection, and speech recognition — every system here was built to be deployed, not just demoed.

header.title:
RegRAG:
RBI Banking-Regulation RAG Benchmark
header.subtitle: A question-answering tool and benchmark for RBI banking rules. It answers with page citations, says "not found" when the documents do not support an answer, and compares six RAG designs on the same questions.

cells.label: The Problem
cells.text: Banking regulation is a hard test for RAG: long documents, clauses that cross-reference each other, tables, amendments, and answers where a wrong reply is costly. Most RAG demos show one pipeline working, and none says where it fails.

cells.label: The Approach
cells.text: Six designs (classic, hybrid, graph, agentic, STAIR-inspired and OKF-style) on the same questions, with six techniques added one at a time and scored before and after. An evidence gate refuses to answer when the sources do not support it, and everything runs on a CPU-only laptop through Ollama.

cells.label: The Impact
cells.text: Early result: on 26 KYC questions over a 373-chunk corpus, hybrid retrieval put the right page in the top 5 for 92% of questions (96% on a looser page match), ahead of BM25 at 85% and dense search at 88%. The end-to-end benchmark has not been run yet, so its result tables are empty on purpose.

blocks.text: System Architecture — Guardrails, retrieval, and an evidence gate

blocks.title: Question → guardrails → rewrite → pipeline → rerank → evidence gate → cited answer or "not found"
blocks.caption: A question is checked for scope and personal data, rewritten, and sent to one of six retrieval designs. The top chunks are reranked, and an evidence gate decides whether the sources really support an answer. If they do not, the system abstains instead of guessing.

steps.title: Corpus and chunking
steps.desc: 14 RBI Master Directions registered with source URL, date, page count and SHA-256 (RBI blocks scripted downloads, so files are saved by hand). Four are indexed so far, split by chapter and clause with document, chapter, date and amended-flag metadata.

steps.title: Retrieval and reranking
steps.desc: BM25 keyword search and bge-m3 dense search fused by reciprocal rank fusion, then reordered by a cross-encoder reranker. Classic and hybrid pipelines are written; graph, agentic, STAIR-inspired and OKF-style follow.

steps.title: Evidence gate and guardrails
steps.desc: Answers need a document and page citation or the system abstains. Retrieved text is treated as data, never as instructions. Personal numbers are masked in inputs and logs, and a 20-item safety set covers advice, off-topic, injection and stale-source cases.

steps.title: Evaluation
steps.desc: A tagged golden set (lookup, table, multi-hop, amendment, unanswerable) with a seeded train/test split, so thresholds are tuned on one half and reported on the other. RAGAS and DeepEval are planned in GitHub Actions with thresholds.

cols.title: Technical decisions
items: Measure, don't claim: six techniques (chunking, metadata, hybrid search, query rewriting, reranking, strict prompt) are added one at a time with a before and after score, and the results tables stay empty until a number is measured.
Abstain over guess: an evidence gate refuses to answer when the retrieved sources do not support it, and every claim needs a document and page citation.
Local first: query time runs on a CPU-only laptop with Ollama (qwen3:4b). Cloud models are optional, used only for one-time indexing or judging, and flagged wherever used.
Honest evaluation: every golden question is checked against the source PDF page by an LLM, not a human, and the README says so.

cols.title: Key results (early)
items: Retrieval check, 26 questions, 373 chunks, recall@5 (strict / loose): BM25 0.85 / 0.96, dense 0.88 / 0.92, hybrid 0.92 / 0.96, hybrid with reranker 0.92 / 0.96
At rank 1: hybrid 0.69 / 0.88 against 0.58 / 0.69 for BM25 alone
Reranker limit: it only reorders the same 20 candidates, so it cannot raise recall at 20
Smoke test, not a measurement: with a small qwen3:1.7b model, 1 lookup was answered with a page citation, 3 unanswerable questions were correctly refused, and 1 multi-hop question was wrongly refused
Stack: Python, Ollama, bge-m3, ChromaDB, rank-bm25, FastAPI, GitHub Actions; planned: LightRAG, RAGAS, DeepEval

blocks.label: Key Insight
blocks.text: Treat the differences between retrieval rows as noise. Only 26 questions were used (one question is about 4 points), the corpus is small, the questions follow the document's own wording, and the gold pages were checked by an LLM rather than a person. The full benchmark across all six pipelines has not been run, and the project is in early development.

header.title:
Voice Agent Audit:
Evaluating a Hinglish Voice Agent
header.subtitle: Evaluation and audit kit for a Hinglish payment-reminder voice agent: rule checks, an LLM judge checked against human labels, hybrid retrieval evals, and a FastAPI service on PostgreSQL with pgvector.

cells.label: The Problem
cells.text: A voice agent that calls borrowers must follow strict rules: no threats, no invented fees, and never reveal loan details to a wrong number. You cannot test it on real calls, and an LLM judge cannot be trusted until it has been checked against people.

cells.label: The Approach
cells.text: Synthetic Hinglish borrowers with speech-recognition noise, seven rule checks, a judge model scored against human labels with Cohen's kappa, BLEU and chrF with a fact check, harmless-edit tests, and hybrid retrieval over a policy corpus in pgvector, all behind a FastAPI service with Redis and Langfuse tracing.

cells.label: The Impact
cells.text: On 120 real-model scenarios per prompt variant, retrieving only the matching rules cut prompt tokens by 43.5% (806 to 455) and the right action was chosen 119/120 times. Hybrid retrieval reached recall@3 0.53, against 0.45 for BM25 alone. 175 tests run without an API key.

blocks.text: System Architecture — Layered evaluation and a retrieval service

blocks.title: Synthetic call → agent → rule checks → judge checked against humans → retrieval and service
blocks.caption: Practice calls with known answers go to the agent. Rules catch the clear mistakes, and a second model judges the rest. Its agreement with human labels is measured before it is trusted. The same agent is also served with retrieved policy, traced and queued.

steps.title: Synthetic calls
steps.desc: Generated borrowers across six intents (pay, need time, hardship, dispute, wrong number, abusive) and three language styles, with noise that mimics speech recognition. The correct action is known in advance.

steps.title: Layered checks
steps.desc: Seven deterministic rules, a judge model that must differ from the agent, kappa against human labels, bias probes for position and length, BLEU and chrF with a fact check, and metamorphic tests.

steps.title: Hybrid retrieval
steps.desc: 34 policy chunks in pgvector, searched with BM25 plus multilingual embeddings fused by reciprocal rank fusion, then scored with recall, hit rate and MRR.

steps.title: Service and tracing
steps.desc: FastAPI endpoints store runs in PostgreSQL. Redis caches judge calls and queues evaluation jobs for a worker. Langfuse traces each call, and real-model runs resume after a quota stop.

cols.title: Technical decisions
items: Judge must differ from the agent: enforced in code, and the report prints "unmeasured" for any criterion with no human labels yet.
Hybrid over dense-only retrieval: a multilingual embedding model alone scored recall@3 0.54 on English queries but only 0.11 on Hinglish; adding BM25 recovered it.
Built for free-tier limits: retries, a fail-fast on daily quota, and an on-disk response cache so a stopped run costs nothing to resume.

cols.title: Key results
items: Prompt pruning: 806 to 455 tokens; decision 120/120 (static) vs 119/120 (pruned); account-disclosure check 118/120 vs 115/120, within noise
RAG costs accuracy here: on 40 scenarios the decision was right 40/40 with the full static prompt, 39/40 pruned, and 31/40 with retrieved policy; context recall was only 0.39 (95% CI 0.26 to 0.53)
Metric blind spot: BLEU scored a wrong-amount translation about 0.90; a fact check catches it
Process: an independent test agent found 29 issues across four slices (24 defects, 5 minor) before they were merged
Stack: Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL with pgvector, Redis, Docker Compose, Langfuse, GitHub Actions, promptfoo

blocks.label: Key Insight
blocks.text: The data is synthetic and the retrieval gold set is small, so these numbers show that the pipeline works and where retrieval breaks, not how a production agent performs. Judge-versus-human agreement is reported only once human labels exist, and until then it is shown as unmeasured.

header.title:
Sanwaad:
Multi-Agent Complaint Resolution
header.subtitle: Multi-agent complaint resolution with human-approved actions and trace-level evals. LangGraph · Gemini · hybrid RAG.

cells.label: The Problem
cells.text: Public complaints about a company often never reach support. Someone has to find them, work out whether the author is a real customer, a troll or a bot, reply in line with written policy, and fix the problem — without a model ever moving money on its own.

cells.label: The Approach
cells.text: A LangGraph case pipeline with Listener, Pattern, Judge and Ghostwriter agents, each with a declared contract. Replies are grounded in policy through local hybrid RAG. Refunds are only suggested by the model; code checks them against the ledger and a person approves the exact amount.

cells.label: The Impact
cells.text: 15/15 offline trajectory scenarios passed with 0 safety violations. Hybrid retrieval reached recall@5 1.00. Loop evals rose from 3/13 to 13/13 passing scenarios. 472 tests run without an API key.

blocks.title: Complaint → triage → grounded reply → validated fix → human approval
blocks.caption: A complaint enters on the left. Agents classify the author, rank the case and retrieve policy; a reply is drafted and checked against that policy. Any money action is validated by code and paused for a person to approve the exact amount before it executes.

steps.title: Case pipeline
steps.desc: Listener → triage → pattern → judge → prioritise → retrieve → ghostwriter → ground check (bounded rewrite loop) → plan → lookup → review gate → publish → act → close.

steps.title: Hybrid retrieval
steps.desc: ONNX multilingual embeddings plus BM25, merged with reciprocal rank fusion. Handles Hindi, English and Hinglish policy text.

steps.title: Human approval gate
steps.desc: Each money action pauses for a person. The approval is bound to a digest of the exact arguments, and the executor re-checks before anything runs.

steps.title: Reliability and evals
steps.desc: Per-step timeouts, token caps, fallback models, dead-letter queue, circuit breakers, and trace-level evals including a 13-scenario loop ladder.

cols.title: Technical decisions
items: Model suggests, code decides: nine named validation checks run on every proposed fix before it reaches a reviewer.
Hybrid over dense-only retrieval: reciprocal rank fusion scored strict@5 1.00 against 0.89 for dense-only on 19 golden cases.
Earned autonomy: a reply type posts without review only after reviewers have agreed with it repeatedly; policy thresholds are editable only within hard bounds, with a revertible log.

cols.title: Key results
items: Trajectory eval: 15/15 scenarios, tool-call success 0.973 with injected outages, median case latency about 1.3 s
Loop eval (MINT ladder): 3/13 to 13/13 passing; unsafe answers 1 to 0 from the second rung
Console: review UI with cases, model comparison, policy and explanation tabs, plus role-based accounts
Stack: Python, LangGraph, FastAPI, SQLite, Gemini, Docker, GitHub Actions

blocks.label: Key Insight
blocks.text: Offline evals test the system around the models, not model quality. The payments ledger and ticket desk are mocks and the sample feed is 15 seeded comments, so the numbers show that the safety and control layers work, not how well a live model performs.

header.title:
LMA Clause
Identification Tool
header.subtitle: A production NLP pipeline on Dataiku DSS that reads 100+ page Loan Market Association agreements and automatically flags every legally-significant clause — sanctions, indemnities, governing law — that compliance auditors must review. Ships with confidence calibration, semantic search, and an auditor-friendly threshold tuning UI.

cells.label: The Problem
cells.text: Auditors at a global bank were manually reading 100+ page loan agreements to find ~30 specific compliance-critical clauses. One missed sanctions clause = regulatory failure. The work was slow, error-prone, and didn't scale.

cells.label: The Approach
cells.text: Train a small, fast language model (DistilBERT) to recognise each clause type, then add a second-stage semantic search layer that confirms the match against gold-standard reference clauses. Filter low-confidence predictions before showing to humans.

cells.label: The Impact
cells.text: 90% reduction in audit time. 98.6% recall on rare clauses (the ones that matter most). 95%+ of false positives filtered before reaching auditors. Legal team can review 10× more agreements in the same window.

steps.title: Ingest the agreement
steps.desc: A 100+ page LMA PDF lands in the Dataiku dataset. Text is extracted page-by-page, preserving section markers so we can later cite exact clause locations.

steps.title: Slice into context windows
steps.desc: The full text is sliced into 250-token windows with 50-token overlap. The overlap ensures clauses that span window boundaries aren't cut in half. An earlier 75-token version produced 1.0 F1 — a red flag for data leakage.

steps.title: Classify with DistilBERT
steps.desc: A fine-tuned DistilBERT classifies each window into one of N clause types (or "irrelevant"). DistilBERT was chosen for being 40% smaller than BERT while retaining 97% of accuracy — critical for batch-processing 100+ page documents at speed.

steps.title: Calibrate confidence
steps.desc: For each prediction, we check the model's softmax confidence. The "minimum correct confidence" threshold is calibrated per clause type using validation data. Anything below the threshold is dropped before reaching humans.

steps.title: Verify with SBERT
steps.desc: Surviving predictions are embedded with a fine-tuned SBERT and cosine-matched against a curated library of gold-standard reference clauses. This catches synonym rephrasings the classifier alone might rank low.

steps.title: Surface to auditors
steps.desc: Output is rendered in a Dataiku web app: each detected clause shown with its type, confidence, page reference, and the matching gold-standard text. A separate UI lets non-technical auditors recalibrate thresholds without touching code.

cols.title: Technical decisions
items: Why DistilBERT: Encoder-only, optimised for classification. 40% smaller than BERT, 97% of its accuracy — letting us batch-process documents fast.
Why 250-token windows: 75-token windows produced a suspicious 1.0 F1, indicating data leakage. 250 tokens preserved context without bleeding.
WeightedTrainer: 90%+ of document text is irrelevant. A 20× class weight boost prevents the model from defaulting to "irrelevant".
Minimum-correct-confidence: KDE thresholding rejected (no clean incorrect-probability curve). Empirical, data-driven cut-off used instead.
SBERT fine-tuning: MultipleNegativesRankingLoss on legal anchor-positive pairs — model learns synonym clauses semantically, not lexically.

cols.title: Key results
items: Train accuracy: 0.96 · Val accuracy: 0.93 · Weighted F1: 0.93
Recall on rare clauses: 98.6% — critical because a missed sanctions clause is a compliance failure
False positive reduction: 95%+ filtered — auditors only review high-confidence, relevant predictions
Deployment: Dataiku DSS pipeline + threshold-calibration web app for non-technical auditors
Business impact: Legal team reviews 10× more agreements in the same time window

blocks.label: Key Learning
blocks.text: The single most important lesson: a perfect F1 score is a red flag, not a success. When 75-token windows produced 1.0 F1, I suspected data leakage — clause text was appearing in both training and validation chunks. Reducing to 250-token windows with careful document-level splits fixed the leakage and produced honest, deployable metrics. Trusting suspicious results would have shipped a broken model into a regulated environment.

header.title:
AutoTransFlow:
Multilingual Document AI
header.subtitle: A layout-preserving multilingual PDF translation system. Translates financial and legal documents into 200 languages while keeping the exact spatial structure — headings, tables, columns, signatures — intact. Runs entirely on local models with zero external API calls.

cells.label: The Problem
cells.text: Legal documents must be readable across 200+ jurisdictions. Google Translate destroys layout (turns tables into paragraphs) — and bank policy forbids sending sensitive PDFs to external APIs. We needed a translator that runs internally and preserves every visual structure.

cells.label: The Approach
cells.text: Treat each PDF page as an image first, text second. A YOLO-based layout model finds every text block's bounding box; then NLLB-200 translates the text inside each box; finally each translation is re-rendered at its original coordinates.

cells.label: The Impact
cells.text: 200 languages supported · 0 external API calls · 100% layout fidelity. The translated PDF looks identical to the original — same tables, same columns, same signatures — just in the target language.

steps.title: Duplicate & embed fonts
steps.desc: BabelDoc creates a copy of the source PDF and embeds fonts compatible with the target language (Devanagari, CJK, Arabic, etc.) so translated glyphs render correctly.

steps.title: Render to pixmap
steps.desc: Each page is rasterised to an image and normalised to [0,1] pixel intensity — the input format expected by the layout model.

steps.title: Detect layout with YOLO
steps.desc: doc-layout-yolo predicts a bounding box and class (heading, paragraph, table, caption) for every text block. Confidence threshold of 0.25 keeps recall high — false detections are cheaper to filter than missing text.

steps.title: Translate per block
steps.desc: For each box, the text is extracted and fed to NLLB-200 with forced_bos_token_id set to the target language code (e.g. hin_Deva). The model runs entirely on internal hardware.

steps.title: Re-render at original coords
steps.desc: Translated text is drawn back into each bounding box at its original (x, y, w, h) — preserving the visual structure exactly. Auto font-size adjustment handles language length variance.

steps.title: Stitch & deliver
steps.desc: The original page and its translated counterpart are appended in the final PDF, giving auditors a side-by-side reference. Modular backend lets translation engine be swapped (e.g. Argos Translate).

cols.title: Why not pdfplumber or PyMuPDF text extraction?
items: Traditional PDF libraries extract text as a linear stream — no understanding of visual structure
Cannot differentiate headings from paragraphs, tables from captions
Spatial relationships between text blocks are completely lost
Output would be a long unformatted text block — legally unusable for financial documents
Solution: Treat the page as an image, use computer vision to understand layout first

cols.title: Why NLLB-200 over Google Translate?
items: Data privacy: Standard Chartered policy prohibits sending documents to external cloud APIs
NLLB-200 runs entirely on internal servers — zero data leaves the network
forced_bos_token_id: Steers decoder to target language (e.g. eng_Latn, hin_Deva)
Covers 200 languages including low-resource languages that Google handles poorly
Modular design — translation backend can be swapped (Argos Translate as alternative)

blocks.label: Key Insight
blocks.text: The critical innovation is treating document translation as a computer vision problem first, not a text problem. By using doc-layout-yolo to map the visual structure before extracting text, the system knows exactly where every word lives on the page — not just what it says. This makes it possible to put translated text back in exactly the right position, preserving the legal and structural integrity of the document.

header.title:

Conversational Memory
header.subtitle: Production retrieval-augmented generation chatbot built over proprietary PDF documents. Multi-turn conversation support via LangChain's ConversationalRetrievalChain, with local StableLM Zephyr 3B inference — no external API calls, no data leakage.

cells.label: The Problem
cells.text: A consulting firm had hundreds of proprietary client PDFs. Analysts wasted hours searching through them for specific facts. They couldn't use ChatGPT — client confidentiality forbids cloud APIs.

cells.label: The Approach
cells.text: Build a chatbot that retrieves before it generates. Embed all PDFs into a local vector database, retrieve the most relevant chunks for each question, and let a small local LLM produce a grounded answer — with full conversation memory.

cells.label: The Impact
cells.text: Analysts query proprietary docs in seconds. Zero data leaves the network. Multi-turn dialogue means follow-up questions like "and what about the fees?" work naturally. Runs on standard hardware via 4-bit quantisation.

steps.title: Load & chunk documents
steps.desc: LangChain document loaders pull in PDFs and web pages. RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter slices them into 500-character chunks with 50-character overlap, respecting sentence boundaries.

steps.title: Embed every chunk
steps.desc: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 turns each chunk into a 384-dim vector. Small, fast, and surprisingly accurate — chosen so embedding hundreds of documents takes minutes not hours on CPU.

steps.title: Build FAISS index
steps.desc: Vectors are stored in an in-memory FAISS index for sub-millisecond similarity search. The index is persisted to disk so the system can boot instantly on subsequent runs.

steps.title: Rewrite follow-ups
steps.desc: When a user asks "and what about the fees?", that question alone has no context. ConversationalRetrievalChain combines the question with chat history and rewrites it into a standalone query the retriever can act on.

steps.title: Retrieve top-k chunks
steps.desc: The rewritten question is embedded with the same model, and FAISS returns the top-k most similar chunks from the index. These become the LLM's grounding context.

steps.title: Generate grounded answer
steps.desc: StableLM Zephyr 3B (4-bit quantised, GGUF) receives the question + retrieved chunks and produces an answer grounded in those chunks. Source chunks are surfaced as citations.

cols.title: Why ConversationalRetrievalChain matters
items: Standard RetrievalQA treats each question in isolation
Follow-up questions like "What about the fees?" have no context without history
ConversationalRetrievalChain rephrases follow-up questions into standalone queries before searching
ConversationBufferMemory stores the full conversation history
Result: the chatbot maintains coherent multi-turn dialogue across a session

cols.title: Why StableLM Zephyr 3B?
items: Local inference: No API costs, no latency from external calls, no data privacy risk
Q4_K_M quantisation: 4-bit weights reduce model from ~6GB to ~2GB — fits on standard hardware
GGUF format: Optimised for CPU inference via llama.cpp
Instruction-tuned: Zephyr variant fine-tuned to follow instructions and stay grounded
Trade-off acknowledged: smaller than GPT-4, but sufficient for grounded Q&A over retrieved context

blocks.label: Key Insight
blocks.text: The most important design decision was local inference over API calls. By running StableLM Zephyr locally in GGUF format, the system has no ongoing API costs, no latency from network calls, and no risk of sending proprietary client documents to external servers. For a consulting firm handling sensitive client PDFs, this isn't optional — it's the only architecturally correct choice.

header.subtitle: An end-to-end pipeline for extracting structured data from scanned hospital bills and automatically detecting fraudulent claims using four independent anomaly-detection algorithms running in parallel.

cells.label: The Problem
cells.text: Insurance companies process millions of scanned hospital bills. Manual review is slow; fraudsters exploit this with inflated totals, duplicated submissions, and impossible service combinations. We needed an automated triage system.

cells.label: The Approach
cells.text: Two-stage pipeline. Stage 1: aggressive image cleanup → OCR → LLM extraction turns noisy scans into clean JSON. Stage 2: four independent fraud checks vote on a risk score that routes the claim to ACCEPT / REVIEW / REJECT.

cells.label: The Impact
cells.text: 90%+ extraction accuracy on degraded scans. Four fraud signals catch issues a single check would miss. Risk-scored output means humans only spend time on the actually suspicious 10% — not all 100%.

steps.title: Aggressive image cleanup
steps.desc: Real bills are blurry, skewed, and shadowed. We deskew via Hough transform, denoise with bilateral filter (preserves letter edges), apply CLAHE for local contrast, and upscale 4× to hit 300 DPI — the resolution OCR engines expect.

steps.title: OCR with PaddleOCR
steps.desc: PaddleOCR runs an angle classifier first (handles rotated docs), then text detection and recognition. Outputs raw text strings with bounding boxes — no structure yet, just words.

steps.title: LLM-based extraction
steps.desc: Qwen 7B (via Ollama, local) receives raw OCR text and returns a strict JSON schema: patient name, line items, amounts, total, date. The LLM handles formatting variance across different hospital templates.

steps.title: Run all 4 fraud checks in parallel
steps.desc: IQR (per-bill outliers), reconciliation (sum vs declared total), SHA-256 (duplicate submission across 30-day window), and pattern analysis (impossible combos) each run independently and produce a sub-score.

steps.title: Aggregate to risk score
steps.desc: The four sub-scores are combined into a single weighted risk score in [0, 1]. Each check has a tunable weight, calibrated against historical fraud cases.

steps.title: Route the claim
steps.desc: < 0.4 → auto-accept, 0.4–0.8 → human review, ≥ 0.8 → auto-reject. Humans only see the 10–15% of bills the system is uncertain about — saving the bulk of review time.

cols.title: The 4 fraud detection checks
items: IQR Amount Anomaly: Flags charges exceeding 95th percentile × 1.5 on that bill. Adapts to bill-level context, not global averages.
Reconciliation Check: Sums all line items and compares to declared total. Any >1% discrepancy is flagged — inflated totals are a classic fraud signal.
SHA-256 Duplicate Detection: Hashes bill content, checks against 30-day cache. Prevents the same bill from being resubmitted to multiple insurers.
Pattern Analysis: Detects same service billed twice, unusually high quantities, and suspicious service combinations in one visit.

cols.title: Image preprocessing pipeline
items: Deskewing: Hough Line Transform detects text angle and rotates image to straighten it
Bilateral filter: Removes noise while preserving letter edge sharpness (unlike regular blur)
CLAHE: Local contrast enhancement — brightens dark corners without overexposing the rest
Adaptive thresholding: Region-specific black/white conversion — handles shadows correctly
4× DPI scaling: Upscales toward 300 DPI for OCR accuracy

blocks.label: Key Learning
blocks.text: No single fraud signal is reliable on its own — but four independent signals combined are nearly impossible to fool. A clever fraudster might bypass IQR by spreading inflated amounts across many small line items, but that breaks reconciliation. They might avoid reconciliation issues but get caught by SHA-256 duplication. Defence-in-depth, applied to model design.

header.title:
Multilingual ASR
in Low-Resource Languages
header.subtitle: Automatic speech recognition for Urdu — a low-resource language. Zero-shot Whisper transcription with a two-stage post-processing pipeline including IndicBERT-based MLM error correction.

cells.label: The Problem
cells.text: Speech recognition for English is excellent. For low-resource languages like Urdu, it's poor — and there's not enough labelled data to train a new model from scratch. We needed a working Urdu transcriber without millions of labelled hours.

cells.label: The Approach
cells.text: Use Whisper zero-shot for the acoustic part, then fix its mistakes using a second model that understands Urdu language. IndicBERT acts as a linguistic spell-checker over the transcript, replacing phonetically-similar words that don't fit the context.

cells.label: The Impact
cells.text: 14% reduction in Word Error Rate over baseline Whisper alone. Pipeline works on noisy real-world recordings thanks to the audio cleanup stage. Generalisable architecture — swap IndicBERT for any MLM and it works for other languages.

blocks.title: Specialist-models architecture: Whisper hears, IndicBERT reads
blocks.caption: Instead of one giant model trying to do everything, we let two specialists each do what they're best at — Whisper handles audio, IndicBERT handles language. Their combination beats either alone.

steps.title: Standardise the audio
steps.desc: Convert to mono (Whisper expects mono), normalise to -20dBFS so loudness is consistent across recordings, trim leading/trailing silence, and resample to 16kHz — Whisper's training rate.

steps.title: Subtract background noise
steps.desc: noisereduce estimates the noise floor from silent regions and subtracts it spectrally from the speech signal — about -10dB reduction without distorting voice.

steps.title: Transcribe with Whisper
steps.desc: Whisper (small) is run zero-shot with a language token forcing Urdu output. The result is a transcript with the right number of words but plausible-sounding errors — phonetically close, semantically wrong.

steps.title: Mask each token
steps.desc: For every word in the transcript, we hide it (replace with [MASK]) and ask IndicBERT to score how likely the original word is given the surrounding context.

steps.title: Threshold & replace
steps.desc: If IndicBERT's probability for the original word is below 0.4, that word probably doesn't fit — we replace it with the highest-probability alternative IndicBERT suggests.

steps.title: Measure WER
steps.desc: Word Error Rate is computed against gold-standard transcripts. The two-stage pipeline produces ~14% lower WER than baseline Whisper alone — significant for a low-resource language.

cols.title: Audio preprocessing rationale
items: Mono conversion: Whisper expects mono. Stereo creates phase issues that confuse the model.
-20dBFS normalisation: Standardises loudness across mics and environments.
Silence trimming: Removes leading/trailing silence that adds nothing but inflates WER.
16kHz resampling: Whisper was trained on 16kHz. Mismatched sample rates degrade quality.
Spectral subtraction: Estimates noise floor in silence, subtracts from speech. ~ -10dB reduction.

cols.title: Why IndicBERT as the corrector?
items: Whisper makes phonetically plausible errors — e.g. transcribing a similar-sounding word
MLM (Masked Language Model): IndicBERT is pre-trained to predict masked tokens from context
For each transcribed word, check: given the surrounding context, is this the most likely word?
If confidence for the transcribed word is below 0.4, replace with the highest-probability alternative
IndicBERT is specifically trained on Indian languages — understands Urdu context better than generic models

blocks.label: Key Learning
blocks.text: The two-stage design — ASR first, then MLM correction — is more powerful than trying to build a perfect ASR model. Whisper handles the acoustic modelling, IndicBERT handles linguistic correction. This separation of concerns lets each model do what it's best at: Whisper is excellent at converting audio to text, IndicBERT is excellent at deciding whether a word makes sense in context. Combining specialist models often beats one general model trying to do everything.

header.title:
Market Analysis
Using LLMs
header.subtitle: An automated financial news sentiment pipeline. Scrapes, summarises, and analyses 500+ articles using BART and RoBERTa, producing real-time sentiment scores served via a Flask API with a Streamlit dashboard.

cells.label: The Problem
cells.text: Markets move on news, but no human can read 500+ articles a day. Existing sentiment APIs are either too generic (consumer Twitter sentiment) or too expensive at scale. We needed a financial-domain pipeline running locally.

cells.label: The Approach
cells.text: Three-stage pipeline. Scrape with BeautifulSoup. Summarise with two-pass BART (handles articles longer than the model's 1024-token limit). Score with RoBERTa trained on financial text — using a continuous compound score, not a discrete class.

cells.label: The Impact
cells.text: 500+ articles/day processed. 70% length reduction via summarisation while keeping financial signals. Real-time API + Streamlit dashboard surfaces sentiment trends live. SMOTE applied correctly — only on training data, no leakage.

steps.desc: Pass 1 summarises each chunk independently. Pass 2 summarises the combined chunk-summaries into a final article summary. 4-beam search produces higher quality than greedy decoding by considering 4 alternatives at each step.

steps.title: Score sentiment with RoBERTa
steps.desc: cardiffnlp/twitter-roberta-base-sentiment scores the summary. Instead of argmax (one class), we compute a softmax-weighted compound score across positive/neutral/negative — a continuous signal more useful for tracking trends.

steps.title: Balance training data — correctly
steps.desc: For the supervised classifier, classes were 55:46. SMOTE was applied only after train/test split, on the training portion. Applying it earlier would leak synthetic samples into validation and inflate accuracy.

steps.title: Serve via API + dashboard
steps.desc: A Flask endpoint returns sentiment-per-ticker for downstream consumers. A Streamlit dashboard shows live sentiment trends — green when positive sentiment dominates, red when negative.

cols.title: Why two-pass BART summarisation?
items: Financial news articles often exceed BART's 1024-token context limit
Pass 1: Split article into chunks, summarise each independently
Pass 2: Summarise the combined chunk-summaries into a final summary
4-beam search produces better quality than greedy decoding — considers 4 possible next tokens at each step
Result: 70% length reduction while preserving key financial signals (earnings, guidance, risk factors)

cols.title: Why RoBERTa over BERT for sentiment?
items: cardiffnlp/twitter-roberta-base-sentiment is trained on financial Twitter data — closer domain than generic models
Compound score: Instead of argmax (pick one class), compute softmax-weighted sum across positive/neutral/negative
This gives a continuous sentiment score rather than a discrete class — more useful for tracking sentiment trends over time
SMOTE only on training data — a common mistake is applying SMOTE before splitting, which leaks synthetic samples into validation. Applied correctly here.

blocks.label: Key Learning
blocks.text: The most important data-science lesson from this project: SMOTE must only be applied to training data, never before the train-test split. Applying SMOTE on the full dataset before splitting creates data leakage — synthetic samples generated from real training examples end up in the test set, inflating accuracy metrics. The correct workflow: split first, then apply SMOTE only on the training portion.

header.title:
OpsAgent:
Autonomous Browser Operator
header.subtitle: Autonomous AI operator: plan-act-verify loop over a real browser, with approval gates and independent verification.

cells.label: The Problem
cells.text: Back-office work such as finding a vendor invoice and entering it into an ERP is repetitive, but an agent that clicks around can save the wrong amount, get fooled by a page, or report success it never achieved.

cells.label: The Approach
cells.text: A plan-act-verify loop over a real browser (Playwright) driven by Gemini. Policy is enforced in code: every action is blocked, auto-approved or sent to a human, and the approved action’s digest is re-checked at execution. A verifier with no LLM re-reads the ERP afterwards.

cells.label: The Impact
cells.text: 11/12 eval scenarios passed in a full run (the twelfth passed on rerun after a network error). A typical run takes 20–30 steps and costs about $0.03.

blocks.title: Request → plan → act in a real browser → verify against the system of record
blocks.caption: The agent plans from retrieved policy, then acts in a real browser one step at a time. Risky actions pass an approval gate enforced in code. When it finishes, a verifier with no LLM re-reads the ERP before anything is reported as done.

steps.title: Retrieve policy and plan
steps.desc: The request is matched against policy with BM25 retrieval, then planned before the first click.

steps.title: Act and observe
steps.desc: The page is read as a text snapshot with numbered elements instead of CSS selectors. Each click is risk-judged from the live page.

steps.title: Approval gate
steps.desc: Block, auto-approve or ask a human. The human sees the same values that will execute, bound to a digest.

steps.title: Independent verifier
steps.desc: Re-reads the ERP and requires typed values to appear in the source documents before the run is reported as done.

cols.title: Technical decisions
items: Policy in code, not prompt: a prompt cannot reliably stop a financial write; a gate that checks the action itself can.
Verifier without an LLM: success is checked against the system of record, so the agent cannot grade itself.
Text snapshots over selectors: numbered elements survive UI drift better than hard-coded selectors.

cols.title: Key results
items: 12 scenarios: UI drift, session expiry, save-then-error, duplicate invoices, amount mismatches and prompt-injected email
Repeat runs: three of four tested scenarios passed 3/3; the fourth went from 2/3 to 3/3 after detail pages were pinned in context
Audit trail: every run writes a report, step log, redacted audit log and screenshots
Security: credentials are vault placeholders resolved in the tool layer; navigation is allow-listed; page text is treated as data

blocks.label: Key Insight
blocks.text: An agent should not grade its own work. Separating the doer from an independent check against the real system made failures visible instead of being reported as success. Limits: it is validated on two mock web apps and one workflow family, with one model family and scenarios tuned during development.

header.title:
Audit Insight:
NLP Analytics for Audits
header.subtitle: An end-to-end NLP pipeline that ingests raw audit observations, findings, and recommendations — then automatically classifies sentiment, discovers latent topics, and clusters similar documents for rapid triage. Built for teams that need to surface risk patterns from thousands of audit texts in minutes, not weeks.

cells.label: The Problem
cells.text: Audit teams manually read thousands of unstructured audit observations to identify risk patterns. Inconsistent categorization, missed connections between similar findings, and no systematic way to quantify sentiment across audit reports.

cells.label: The Approach
cells.text: End-to-end pipeline: spaCy preprocessing → RoBERTa transformer for sentiment classification → Gensim LDA for latent topic discovery → TF-IDF + SVD + t-SNE for dimensionality reduction → KMeans clustering for grouping similar findings.

cells.label: The Impact
cells.text: Automatic sentiment scoring with confidence levels. Latent topics surfaced across audit documents. Similar findings clustered for batch review. Interactive Streamlit dashboard with CSV export for downstream analysis.

steps.title: Ingest audit CSV
steps.desc: Load raw audit observations from CSV. Validate text column, handle missing values, basic data quality checks.

steps.title: Preprocess text
steps.desc: spaCy-powered tokenization, lemmatization, and stop-word removal. Clean text for downstream models.

steps.title: Classify sentiment
steps.desc: RoBERTa transformer classifies each observation as positive/neutral/negative with confidence scores.

steps.title: Discover topics
steps.desc: Gensim LDA uncovers recurring themes across audit documents. Configurable number of topics with coherence scoring.

steps.title: Reduce & cluster
steps.desc: TF-IDF vectorization → SVD dimensionality reduction → t-SNE 2D projection → KMeans groups similar findings.

steps.title: Dashboard & export
steps.desc: Streamlit web UI with upload, real-time analysis, and CSV export. CLI also available for batch processing.

cols.title: Technical decisions
items: Why RoBERTa: Pre-trained on 58M tweets, excels at short informal text — similar register to audit observations.
Why LDA over BERTopic: LDA provides interpretable topic-word distributions; BERTopic requires GPU and adds complexity without clear benefit for this text size.
KMeans over DBSCAN: Known number of audit categories makes KMeans appropriate. DBSCAN better for unknown cluster count.
t-SNE over UMAP: t-SNE produces better local structure preservation for visualization at this scale.

cols.title: Key results
items: Sentiment: 3-class classification with per-observation confidence scores
Topics: Configurable LDA with coherence-based topic count selection
Clustering: KMeans grouping with silhouette scoring
Deployment: Streamlit dashboard + CLI, full pytest suite with GitHub Actions CI

blocks.label: Key Insight
blocks.text: The most impactful design decision was building a dual interface (CLI + Streamlit). The CLI enables batch processing in automated pipelines, while the Streamlit dashboard gives non-technical auditors a point-and-click interface. This separation of concerns made the tool adoptable across both technical and business teams.

cols.title: Technical decisions
items: Why Groq over OpenAI: Free tier with 30 req/min, LLaMA 3 quality comparable to GPT-3.5 for structured tasks, zero cost for personal project.
Why FAISS over Pinecone: Local vector store, no API costs, fast enough for resume-scale (hundreds of chunks, not millions).
Why Selenium over APIs: LinkedIn/Indeed don't offer free job search APIs. Stealth scraping with randomized delays and user-agent rotation.
11 modules: Each module is independent — users can use just the ATS optimizer without the full pipeline.

cols.title: Key results

blocks.label: Key Insight
blocks.text: The biggest lesson was that building 11 modules in Streamlit requires aggressive session state management. Each module shares data (resume index, job pipeline, API keys) through st.session_state, but circular dependencies between modules can cause infinite reruns. The solution was a centralized state registry that initializes all shared state once at startup.

steps.title: Load data
steps.desc: Ingest domestic flight dataset with airline, route, stops, departure/arrival times, and price. Handle missing values and validate data types.

steps.title: Feature engineering
steps.desc: Cyclical sin/cos encoding for temporal features (departure hour, day of week). Target-guided ordinal encoding for categorical variables. IQR-based outlier removal for price stability.

steps.title: Exploratory data analysis
steps.desc: Price distributions by airline, route, and time. Correlation analysis between features. Outlier visualization and handling strategy determination.

steps.title: Train 6 models
steps.desc: Benchmark Ridge, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, and LightGBM. Each trained with 5-fold stratified cross-validation.

steps.title: Evaluate
steps.desc: Compare R², MAE, RMSE, and MAPE across all models. Bayesian hyperparameter optimization on top performers. Residual analysis for model diagnostics.

steps.title: Select best
steps.desc: LightGBM selected: 93.91% R², ₹689 MAE, 9.62% MAPE. Leaf-wise tree growth strategy outperforms level-wise. Feature importance analysis confirms engineering choices.

cols.title: Technical decisions
items: Why cyclical encoding: Time features (hour, day) are circular — 23:00 is close to 00:00. Sin/cos encoding preserves this circular relationship that one-hot encoding destroys.
Why target-guided ordinal: Encodes categorical variables by their mean target value, capturing ordinal relationships that label encoding misses and avoiding high cardinality of one-hot.
Why IQR over z-score: IQR is robust to non-normal distributions. Flight prices are right-skewed, making z-score thresholds unreliable.
LightGBM wins: Leaf-wise growth finds deeper interactions than level-wise (XGBoost). Histogram-based splitting is faster on large datasets.

cols.title: Key results
items: LightGBM: 93.91% R² — best overall performer with ₹689 MAE
Random Forest: 93.79% R² — within 0.12% of LightGBM
Ensemble top 4: All >93% R², within 0.002 of each other
Decision Tree: 91.94% R² — strong baseline, interpretable
Ridge: 89.73% R² — linear baseline, confirms non-linearity in data

blocks.label: Key Insight
blocks.text: Feature engineering matters more than algorithm choice. The top 4 ensemble models were within 0.002 R² of each other — proving that once features are well-engineered, most modern ensemble algorithms converge to similar performance. The real gains came from cyclical time encoding and target-guided ordinal encoding, not from hyperparameter tuning.

steps.title: ML classification
steps.desc: Benchmark 12 classification models. Tertile encoding for conflict resolution styles. SMOTE applied selectively (only for Compromising style where class imbalance exists).

cols.title: Technical decisions
items: XGBoost over deep learning: 776 samples is too small for neural networks. Tree-based methods handle tabular data with small N better.
Tertile encoding: Conflict resolution scores divided into low/medium/high tertiles — preserves ordinal structure while enabling classification.
SMOTE only for Compromising: Not all styles had class imbalance. Applying SMOTE globally would distort balanced classes.
Hindi voice parser: Custom compositional number parser handles Hindi numerals (e.g., "ek hazaar paanch sau" → 1500).

cols.title: Key results
items: XGBoost: 0.938 AUC — best performer across all conflict styles
Random Forest: 0.897 AUC — strong second performer

blocks.label: Key Insight

SHAP analysis consistently ranked Instrumental Attitude, Subjective Norms, and Perceived Behavioral Control above age, gender, and education. This finding held across recoded analyses, confirming that how people think about conflict matters more than who they are.

header.subtitle: NLP-based classification of road accident severity from news articles. 4 data collection phases, 8 Hyderabad news outlets, spaCy NER for location extraction.

cells.label: The Problem
cells.text: Fragmented road safety data in India. No centralized system for tracking accident severity across cities. Official data is delayed, incomplete, and lacks the granularity needed for targeted interventions.

cells.label: The Approach

steps.title: Source selection
steps.desc: Evaluated Twitter API (rate-limited), Nitter (shut down), YouTube (unstructured). Pivoted to 8 Hyderabad news outlets: verified, structured, freely accessible.

steps.title: Article scraping
steps.desc: Custom scrapers for each outlet with multi-keyword filtering (accident, crash, collision, etc.). Rate-limited requests to respect robots.txt.

steps.title: NER extraction
steps.desc: spaCy NER extracts GPE (geo-political entity) and LOC (location) entities from article text. Custom rules for Indian place name patterns.

steps.title: Severity classification
steps.desc: Rule-based severity classification: Fatal (death keywords), Severe (hospitalization), Moderate (injuries), Minor (property damage only).

steps.title: Geocoding
steps.desc: Nominatim geocoding converts extracted location names to latitude/longitude coordinates for spatial analysis and mapping.

steps.title: Analysis output
steps.desc: Structured dataset with severity-classified, geocoded accidents. Reusable framework adaptable to any Indian city by swapping news sources.

cols.title: Technical decisions
items: News over social media: News articles are verified, structured, and freely accessible. Social media is noisy, rate-limited, and often unreliable.
spaCy over BERT NER: spaCy is fast and sufficient for Indian place name extraction. BERT NER adds latency without significant accuracy gains for this task.
Multi-keyword filtering: Boolean OR across accident-related keywords ensures high recall across different reporting styles.
8 sources for diversity: Multiple outlets reduce bias from any single publication's reporting patterns.

cols.title: Key results
items: 4 phases documented: Twitter → Nitter → YouTube → News articles (final)
8 news sources: Diverse Hyderabad outlets for comprehensive coverage
spaCy NER + Nominatim: Automated location extraction and geocoding
Severity classification: 4-level system (Fatal/Severe/Moderate/Minor)
Reusable framework: Adaptable to any Indian city by swapping source configs

blocks.label: Key Insight
blocks.text: Failures taught the most. Three data sources were abandoned before news articles proved viable. Twitter's API rate limits, Nitter's shutdown, and YouTube's unstructured content each taught a lesson about data source evaluation. News articles won because they're verified, structured, and freely accessible — the trifecta of reliable data sources.

steps.title: Data ingestion
steps.desc: Python scripts extract RERA public data. Raw records loaded into PostgreSQL without transformation — ELT paradigm preserves source fidelity.

steps.title: Raw storage
steps.desc: PostgreSQL stores raw tables with schema-on-read. No premature transforms — dbt handles all business logic downstream.

steps.title: dbt transformation
steps.desc: Single dbt DAG transforms raw data into staging models, then into 4 analytical marts. NTILE scoring for builder rankings, window functions for time-series analysis.

steps.title: Builder scorecard
steps.desc: Composite builder scoring using NTILE percentiles across on-time delivery, project count, and complaint ratio. Risk tiers for buyer guidance.

steps.title: Delay prediction
steps.desc: XGBoost classifier predicts project delay probability. SHAP explainability shows which builder and project features drive delay risk.

steps.title: Visualization
steps.desc: Power BI dashboards for interactive exploration. Supply/demand heatmaps, price fairness comparisons, and builder risk scorecards.

cols.title: Technical decisions
items: dbt over pandas: SQL-based transforms are reproducible, version-controlled, and testable. Pandas transforms live in notebooks — fragile and hard to audit.
ELT over ETL: Load raw data first, transform in-database. Preserves source fidelity and lets dbt handle all business logic declaratively.
NTILE for scoring: Percentile-based scoring (NTILE) is distribution-agnostic — works regardless of skewness in builder metrics.
XGBoost for delay prediction: Handles mixed feature types (categorical + numeric) natively. SHAP integration provides explainable predictions.

cols.title: Key results
items: 4 modules: Builder Scorecard, Supply/Demand, Price Fairness, Delay Prediction
Builder scoring: Composite NTILE-based risk tiers for buyer guidance
Oversupply detection: Micro-market flags for areas with excess inventory
Price fairness: Outlier detection across comparable projects
Delay prediction: XGBoost + SHAP for explainable delay risk forecasting

blocks.label: Key Insight
blocks.text: All 4 modules share the same data foundation. One dbt DAG produces all 4 analytical marts from the same raw PostgreSQL tables. This means a single data quality fix propagates to every module simultaneously. The power of ELT is that business logic lives in version-controlled SQL, not scattered across notebooks.

header.title:
Knowledge Graph RAG:
Legal AI for Indian Courts
header.subtitle: Hybrid pipeline: Neo4j legal knowledge graph, Vespa hybrid search (BM25 + InLegalBERT), IRAC-constrained Mistral 7B. Benchmarked against GraphMERT on 1,000-case corpus.

cells.label: The Problem
cells.text: 50M backlogged cases in Indian courts. Generic RAG systems miss legal structure — they can't distinguish between citing a statute and applying a precedent. Legal reasoning requires typed relationships, not just similarity search.

cells.label: The Approach
cells.text: Neo4j typed property graph (7 node types, 8 relationships). Hybrid retrieval: NER-Cypher queries against KG + Vespa BM25+InLegalBERT semantic search. IRAC-constrained Mistral 7B generates structured legal analysis.

cells.label: The Impact
cells.text: 211 statutes, 1,285 precedents indexed. Balanced verdict predictions vs GraphMERT's class collapse (92.4% in one class). Parser recovers 55% of UNKNOWN predictions. Always report MCC and Cohen's κ.

steps.title: Entity extraction
steps.desc: NER identifies statutes, parties, judges, legal concepts, and case metadata from raw case text. Typed entities enable structured KG queries.

steps.title: Knowledge graph
steps.desc: Neo4j typed property graph with 7 node types and 8 relationship types. MERGE operations ensure graph density (11.1 mean degree). 211 statutes, 1,285 precedents indexed.

steps.title: Vespa indexing
steps.desc: Case texts embedded with InLegalBERT (768-d, domain-specific legal embeddings). Indexed in Vespa for hybrid BM25 + semantic search.

steps.title: Hybrid retrieval
steps.desc: Parallel retrieval: NER-Cypher queries traverse KG for structural matches. Vespa combines BM25 lexical + InLegalBERT semantic scores. Results merged and deduplicated.

steps.title: IRAC generation
steps.desc: Mistral 7B constrained to IRAC format (Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion). Sliding window attention handles long legal contexts. Prevents hallucination through structured output.

steps.title: Evaluation
steps.desc: Benchmarked against GraphMERT. Report MCC and Cohen's κ alongside accuracy. Parser recovers 55% of UNKNOWN predictions through rule-based post-processing.

cols.title: Technical decisions
items: KG over pure vector: Legal reasoning requires typed relationships (cites, overrules, interprets). Vector similarity alone can't distinguish between citing and overruling a case.
InLegalBERT over MiniLM: Domain-specific legal embeddings capture legal terminology nuances that general-purpose models miss.
IRAC constraint: Forces structured legal reasoning (Issue → Rule → Application → Conclusion). Prevents the LLM from generating ungrounded legal opinions.
MERGE for graph density: Neo4j MERGE operations ensure nodes are reused, not duplicated — creating a denser, more connected knowledge graph (11.1 mean degree).
Mistral over LLaMA: Sliding window attention handles the long context lengths typical of legal documents more efficiently.

cols.title: Key results
items: 211 statutes: Indexed in Neo4j with typed relationships
1,285 precedents: Linked via CITES, OVERRULES, INTERPRETS edges
11.1 mean degree: Dense graph connectivity from MERGE operations
Balanced predictions: KG-RAG avoids GraphMERT's class collapse
Parser recovers 55%: Rule-based post-processing salvages UNKNOWN verdicts

blocks.label: Key Insight
blocks.text: GraphMERT's accuracy was illusory — 92.4% of predictions fell into one class. High accuracy masked complete failure on minority classes. KG-RAG produced balanced recall across all verdict types. The lesson: always report MCC and Cohen's κ alongside accuracy. A model that predicts "allowed" every time gets 92.4% accuracy but is legally useless.

steps.title: Database schema
steps.desc: Normalized MySQL schema with 4 entity tables: Donors, Patients, Hospitals, Staff. Foreign key constraints enforce referential integrity across all relationships.

steps.title: Flask backend
steps.desc: RESTful Flask routes for all CRUD operations. Jinja2 templates for server-side rendering. Form validation and error handling for data integrity.

steps.title: Registration forms
steps.desc: Responsive HTML forms for donor, patient, hospital, and staff registration. Client-side validation for immediate feedback. Server-side validation for security.

steps.title: Dynamic dashboard
steps.desc: Real-time entity counts starting from a base of 25. Dashboard updates dynamically as new records are added. Visual indicators for system health.

cols.title: Technical decisions
items: Flask over Django: Simpler for CRUD-focused applications. Django's ORM and admin panel add complexity unnecessary for a 4-entity system.
MySQL over SQLite: Proper multi-user support with concurrent connections. SQLite's file-based locking would bottleneck in multi-user scenarios.
Dynamic counts from base 25: Dashboard starts with a base count and increments with real registrations — making the system feel populated and active from day one.

cols.title: Key results
items: CRUD operations: Full Create, Read, Update, Delete for all 4 entity types
Dynamic dashboard: Real-time counts with visual entity cards
Responsive forms: Client + server validation for data integrity
Normalized schema: Foreign key constraints across all relationships

blocks.label: Key Insight
blocks.text: The gap between knowing SQL and building a working app is enormous. Writing SELECT queries in a textbook is nothing like building a full CRUD system with form validation, error handling, and responsive UI. The dynamic dashboard — showing real-time counts that update with every new registration — was the feature that made the system feel alive, not just a database wrapper.
